In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fault zone contains lineations that are the result of smearing of friction‐weak material along the slip‐parallel direction.
the fault zone is a narrow zone, 1 to 3 km wide, containing lineations of hypocenters that are parallel to the slip direction.
the fault zone is composed of two major components, a narrow fault core and a broader fault zone that contains the fault core and is composed of a series of fault strands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fault zone is characterized by an active fault plane and a weak fault zone material that is not in equilibrium with the fault slip direction, and that this material may be responsible for the observed lineations.
a fault can be considered a “seismic” fault if it has a well‐developed slip‐parallel seismic lineation.
the seismic lineations on our fault zone are a result of the smears of frictionally weak gouge material along the fault zone over thousands of years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the slip‐parallel lineations are a manifestation of the long‐term evolution of the fault, and thus they may provide a useful proxy for fault slip history.
the seismicity structure of a fault can provide a window into the fault’s long‐term slip history.
the slip‐parallel seismicity lineations are the result of long‐term slip‐parallel smearing of frictional weak material.
